sentences.text: Sidonie went home and did not tell her grandfather for two days, and when she did tell him he sat at the table for a while and then went out to the shed and did not come back in for an hour.
Here is what neither of them has ever been able to establish.
Whether the toad did anything.
Whether an eleven-year-old in a ditch in September 1944 was right about seven minutes, or whether she was a frightened child with no watch who has had eighty years to make the number tidy.
Whether a wood can run late.

Whether the whole of it is a hundred and forty pages of one careful man's measurements against tables that were, in fact, slightly wrong for that valley all along, which is the explanation Sidonie's mother offers and which nobody in the family has ever been able to knock over.
What they did establish is why nobody would say.
It is not superstition and it is not shame.
Sidonie worked it out on the walk home from Madame Grandjean's and she has never had a better version of it.
If you say out loud that the wood is seven minutes slow, then the next thing anybody says is: *shouldn't it be put right?* And there is no way to answer that question.

There is no mechanism for putting it right, and there is nobody to ask, and there is a toad under the third stone up from the ford who has done one thing, once, extremely well, at a moment when it counted more than anything else that happened in that valley that year — and who has apparently not given the seven minutes back, and who is not going to, and who has never once been consulted about any of it.
So they leave it.
Sidonie has tested this on herself more than once and it holds.

Every time she gets as far as imagining saying it out loud to somebody at the village hall, the next sentence in her head is *and what are we going to do about it* — and there is nothing to do about it, and the only thing that can happen is that a valley which has got on perfectly well for eighty years starts having a difficult conversation with itself about a toad.

Every forester of the Bois de Herbeuval since Pirlot has known and has said nothing, and the notebook has been handed on twice now and has a hundred and sixty pages, and the whole of it still sits seven minutes behind the tables.
Sidonie is the forester there now.
She took it in 2019.
She measures it in May and September, which is more than her grandfather did, and she writes it in the same notebook in a hand nothing like his.

She has never mentioned it to anybody in the village, and last summer a boy from the last house before the ford asked her a very direct question at the edge of the wood, and she went quiet, and was pleasant, and started talking about something else with real warmth.
She heard herself do it and she has thought about it since.
She is fairly sure she will tell him.
Not this year.
